newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Drug fighters in Caribbean face shifting rings.
newsitem.headline: Drug fighters in Caribbean face shifting rings.

text.p: Boat crews who switch drug pickup points with lightning speed from one island to another are typical of the tight organisation that bedevils U.S. efforts to control Caribbean drug rings, officials say.
The region, which has independent nations as well as U.S., French, British and Dutch island territories, offers myriad possibilities for cocaine, heroin and immigrant smugglers to elude authorities.

Late last year, a U.S. Coast Guard crew was chasing a boat loaded with drugs on its way west to Puerto Rico. When the vessel got wind it was being pursued, it suddenly headed north to one of the British Virgin Islands. There it was met by a pickup truck, which disappeared -- with the boat's crew and its contents -- before police could arrive.

On another night, the local Coast Guard learned of an air drop near the island of Saint Christopher and headed out to meet the motorboat that had picked up the loot. But the traffickers had contingency plans and an organised backup network. One of them pulled out a cellular telephone, made a call and arranged a quick pickup and getaway on an island beyond the jurisdiction of the Saint Christopher crew.

"They will run very fast in one direction and then stop," Capt. Thomas Bernard, commander of the Coast Guard's Greater Antilles Section, told Reuters at the San Juan Coast Guard base. "It's amazing how quickly they can make arrangements."

U.S. authorities say such events illustrate the international organisation of drug traffickers in the Caribbean, even at a time when the United States has enjoyed some success with its stepped-up enforcement in the region.

"Most (of the traffickers) are tied to cartels in Colombia," Bernard said. He said most of the boat crews the Coast Guard picks up, while they are believed to be working for Colombians, are from the Dominican Republic, the Spanish-speaking nation just west of Puerto Rico that shares Hispaniola island with Haiti.
"The great majority of the traffickers in this region are Dominican," Bernard said.

With law enforcement at the U.S. border with Mexico increased, the Caribbean became a natural alternate route for traffickers seeking to ship cocaine and heroin to the United States from South America. Authorities say the region is also a route to the European Union.

For example, planes can take drug shipments from Puerto Rico, a U.S. commonwealth, without facing a customs barrier before reaching the U.S. mainland, and they can reach France from the French islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique, Britain from the Virgin Islands and other British territories and the Netherlands from Dutch outposts such as St. Maarten.
"You have a true international community here, which makes it attractive for them and difficult for us," Bernard said.

U.S. officials say pressure from Europe helped increase the number of islands that have signed agreements to allow the Coast Guard to pursue suspected traffickers into their territorial waters and airspace. Mostly due to concerns about sovereignty, Martinique, Guadeloupe, Haiti, Jamaica and Barbados have not signed such agreements, which has become a diplomatic bone of contention.

To fight the trafficking, Washington last year launched "Operation Frontier Shield," an interagency task force to fight drug and immigrant smuggling. In its first three months, which began on Oct. 1, the task force seized almost 14,000 pounds (6,350 kgs) of cocaine and heroin.
The seizures have continued. During the week that ended last Sunday, more than 6,000 pounds (2,722 kgs) of cocaine was seized, Bernard said.

The stakes are high. Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Rossello estimated this week that eight out of 10 murders on the island are related to drugs and the drug trade. By Thursday, police said, the island had seen some 80 killings in January alone.
